phase-diagram-001.question: At constant pressure, how many degrees of freedom are there at the eutectic point of a binary system (where a liquid and two solid phases coexist)?
phase-diagram-001.explanation: Gibbs' phase rule is F = C − P + 2, but for condensed systems at constant pressure we use F = C − P + 1. At the eutectic point of a binary system (C = 2), three phases, liquid L, α and β, coexist (P = 3), so F = 2 − 3 + 1 = 0: an invariant point at which the temperature and the composition of every phase are fixed. That is why an alloy of eutectic composition solidifies at a single temperature and its cooling curve shows a thermal arrest. One results from applying F = C − P + 2, which includes pressure as a variable, to a constant-pressure phase diagram. Two is the number of degrees of freedom in a single-phase region (P = 1), where temperature and composition can be varied independently.

phase-diagram-002.question: Which binary system is the classic example of an isomorphous phase diagram, with complete solubility in both the liquid and the solid over all compositions?
choices: The Pb-Sn system
The Cu-Ni system
The Fe-C system
phase-diagram-002.explanation: Cu and Ni are both FCC, differ in atomic radius by only about 2%, and have similar electronegativities and valences, so they satisfy the Hume-Rothery rules and form a substitutional solid solution at all compositions. The phase diagram is isomorphous, with a lens-shaped two-phase region bounded by two curves, the liquidus and the solidus. The Pb-Sn system has limited solid solubility and is the classic eutectic system, with a eutectic point at 183 °C. In the Fe-C system, carbon dissolves interstitially with low solubility, giving a complex diagram that includes eutectic, eutectoid and peritectic reactions.

phase-diagram-003.question: A Cu-35 wt% Ni alloy is held at a temperature where two phases coexist: liquid (31.5 wt% Ni) and solid α (42.5 wt% Ni). Which value is closest to the mass fraction of liquid?
choices: About 0.32
About 0.68
About 0.82
phase-diagram-003.explanation: With the lever rule, the fraction of a phase is the distance from the alloy composition to the composition of the opposite phase, divided by the total length of the tie line. The liquid fraction is W_L = (Cα − C₀)/(Cα − C_L) = (42.5 − 35)/(42.5 − 31.5) = 7.5/11.0 ≈ 0.68. About 0.32 is the mistake of taking the distance on the same side, (35 − 31.5)/11.0, which is the fraction of α. About 0.82 is the ratio of the alloy composition to the solid composition, 35/42.5, which is not the lever rule. The fractions of the two phases always sum to 1, which you can use as a check once you have found one of them.

phase-diagram-004.question: In the Pb-Sn system, take the eutectic temperature as 183 °C, the eutectic composition as 61.9 wt% Sn, and the compositions of the α and β phases at that temperature as 18.3 wt% Sn and 97.8 wt% Sn. When a 30 wt% Sn alloy is cooled under equilibrium to just below the eutectic temperature, which value is closest to the mass fraction of the microstructure that is eutectic structure?
choices: About 0.27
About 0.73
About 0.15
phase-diagram-004.explanation: The eutectic structure is what the liquid (61.9 wt% Sn) remaining just above the eutectic temperature turns into through the eutectic reaction. So apply the lever rule in the α + L region just above the eutectic temperature: W_eutectic = W_L = (30 − 18.3)/(61.9 − 18.3) = 11.7/43.6 ≈ 0.27. About 0.73 is the fraction of the remaining primary α, the mistake of taking the opposite distance. About 0.15 is the fraction of all β phase just below the eutectic temperature, (30 − 18.3)/(97.8 − 18.3). All the β is inside the eutectic structure, but the eutectic structure also contains α, so the two do not match. The key to this kind of problem is distinguishing microconstituents (primary and eutectic) from phases (α and β).

phase-diagram-005.question: Which equation represents a peritectic reaction? Write it in the direction of cooling.
choices: L → α + β
γ → α + β
L + α → β
phase-diagram-005.explanation: A peritectic reaction is one in which, on cooling, the liquid L reacts with a previously formed solid α to produce a different solid β: L + α → β. The name comes from the new β phase forming around the α grains as if wrapping them. In the Fe-C system δ + L → γ occurs at about 1495 °C, and peritectics are common in the Cu-Zn and Cu-Sn systems. L → α + β is the eutectic reaction, in which two solids form simultaneously from the liquid, and γ → α + β is the eutectoid reaction, in which two solids form from a solid (such as γ → α + Fe₃C in the Fe-C system). In a peritectic reaction, the β product coats the α and hinders diffusion, so in real solidification the reaction does not go to completion and α tends to remain.

phase-diagram-006.question: Which statement about the eutectoid point of the Fe-Fe₃C phase diagram is correct?
choices: At about 0.76 wt% C and 727 °C, γ → α + Fe₃C occurs and pearlite forms
At about 4.3 wt% C and 1147 °C, L → γ + Fe₃C occurs and lamellar pearlite forms
At about 0.022 wt% C and 912 °C, γ → α occurs and bainite forms
phase-diagram-006.explanation: The eutectoid point of the Fe-Fe₃C system is at about 0.76 wt% C and 727 °C, where austenite (γ) transforms into pearlite, a lamellar structure of ferrite (α) and cementite (Fe₃C). The reaction at about 4.3 wt% C and 1147 °C is the eutectic reaction involving the liquid, and the structure it produces is ledeburite, not pearlite. 0.022 wt% C is the maximum solubility of carbon in α at 727 °C, and 912 °C is the γ → α transformation temperature of pure iron. Bainite does not appear on the equilibrium phase diagram; it is a nonequilibrium structure that forms from undercooled austenite in an intermediate temperature range. Steels with less carbon than the eutectoid composition are called hypoeutectoid, and those with more are called hypereutectoid.

phase-diagram-007.question: A 0.40 wt% C hypoeutectoid steel is cooled under equilibrium to just below 727 °C. Which value is closest to the mass fraction of proeutectoid ferrite? Take the eutectoid composition as 0.76 wt% C, the carbon content of ferrite at 727 °C as 0.022 wt% C, and cementite as 6.70 wt% C.
choices: About 0.51
About 0.94
About 0.49
phase-diagram-007.explanation: Proeutectoid ferrite is the ferrite already formed in the α + γ region just above 727 °C, and all the remaining γ becomes pearlite. From the lever rule, W_proeutectoid α = (0.76 − 0.40)/(0.76 − 0.022) = 0.36/0.738 ≈ 0.49. About 0.51 is the fraction of the remaining pearlite, the mistake of taking the opposite distance. About 0.94 is the fraction of all ferrite treating the steel as the two phases α + Fe₃C, (6.70 − 0.40)/(6.70 − 0.022), which includes the ferrite inside the pearlite as well. The area ratio of proeutectoid ferrite to pearlite in a micrograph is a clue for estimating the carbon content of a hypoeutectoid steel.

phase-diagram-008.question: When a 1.2 wt% C hypereutectoid steel is slowly cooled from the austenite region, what microstructure is obtained at room temperature?
choices: Proeutectoid ferrite and pearlite
Proeutectoid cementite and pearlite
Pearlite only
phase-diagram-008.explanation: In a hypereutectoid steel, with more carbon than the eutectoid composition of 0.76 wt% C, crossing the Acm line during cooling first precipitates proeutectoid cementite as a network along the austenite grain boundaries. On reaching 727 °C, the remaining austenite (about 0.76 wt% C) becomes pearlite through the eutectoid reaction, so the room-temperature microstructure is proeutectoid cementite and pearlite. Proeutectoid ferrite and pearlite is the microstructure of a hypoeutectoid steel, and pearlite alone forms in a eutectoid steel. Because a grain-boundary cementite network causes brittleness, tool steels and similar grades are given a spheroidizing anneal to make the cementite globular.

phase-diagram-009.question: What is the main reason the maximum solubility of carbon is much larger in γ-iron (about 2.14 wt%) than in α-iron (about 0.022 wt%)?
choices: γ-iron has a lower packing factor than α-iron, so its total interstitial volume is larger
In γ-iron, carbon dissolves not interstitially but by substituting for iron atoms
The octahedral interstitial site of FCC γ-iron is larger than any interstitial site in BCC α-iron
phase-diagram-009.explanation: Carbon is an interstitial element that sits in the interstitial sites of iron. A sphere fitting the octahedral site of FCC γ-iron has a radius about 0.41 times that of the iron atom, whereas in BCC α-iron even the largest site, the tetrahedral site, is only about 0.29 times, and the octahedral site about 0.15 times. γ-iron can therefore accommodate carbon with less distortion. FCC actually has the higher packing factor (about 0.74, against about 0.68 for BCC), so the total interstitial volume is larger in BCC, and citing the packing factor gets it backward. What matters is that in BCC the free space is divided into many small holes. Carbon dissolves interstitially, not substitutionally.

phase-diagram-010.question: When a Cu-Ni alloy is cooled under equilibrium through the temperature range where liquid and solid coexist, how do the compositions of the liquid and solid change?
choices: Both shift toward the Ni-rich side
Both shift toward the Ni-poor (Cu) side
The solid shifts toward the Ni-rich side and the liquid toward the Cu side
phase-diagram-010.explanation: In a two-phase region, the composition of each phase is given by the ends of the tie line at that temperature: the liquid on the liquidus and the solid on the solidus. In the Cu-Ni system, the liquidus and solidus are higher toward the side of Ni, which has the higher melting point (about 1455 °C), so as the temperature falls both ends of the tie line move toward Cu, which has the lower melting point (about 1085 °C). Both the solid and the liquid therefore lose Ni on cooling, while the amount of solid grows. The idea that the solid shifts toward Ni is a misconception arising from the fact that the first solid to form is Ni-rich. The overall alloy composition does not change, which is consistent with the lever rule showing the solid fraction increasing.

phase-diagram-011.question: When a Cu-Ni alloy is solidified with rapid cooling, as in actual casting, which correctly describes the composition at the center of a dendrite?
choices: Richer in Ni than the average alloy composition
Richer in Cu than the average alloy composition, with the outer parts richer in Ni
Always equal to the average composition, because diffusion in the solid is fast enough
phase-diagram-011.explanation: The solid that forms early in solidification has the composition at the end of the higher-temperature tie line, so it is rich in Ni. With rapid cooling, diffusion in the solid cannot keep up, and the outer layers that solidify later are progressively richer in Cu, leaving segregation in which the composition changes from the center of the dendrite outward (a cored structure, or coring). The center is therefore richer in Ni than the average composition. Diffusion in the solid is far slower than in the liquid, so the equilibrium composition is not necessarily reached. The last regions to solidify have a lower melting point and may melt locally on reheating, so a homogenizing anneal is used to reduce the segregation.

phase-diagram-012.question: The Al-Si system has a eutectic point at 577 °C and 12.6 wt% Si; at that temperature the Si solubility of the α (Al) phase is 1.65 wt%, and the Si phase can be taken as essentially pure Si (100 wt%). When an 18 wt% Si hypereutectic alloy is cooled under equilibrium to just above the eutectic temperature, which value is closest to the mass fraction of primary Si?
choices: About 5.4%
About 16.6%
About 6.2%
phase-diagram-012.explanation: Just above the eutectic temperature, primary Si coexists with liquid of the eutectic composition (12.6 wt% Si). From the lever rule, W_primary Si = (18 − 12.6)/(100 − 12.6) = 5.4/87.4 ≈ 0.062, or about 6.2%. About 5.4% takes the composition difference 18 − 12.6 directly as a percentage without dividing by the length of the tie line. About 16.6% is the fraction of all Si phase just below the eutectic temperature, (18 − 1.65)/(100 − 1.65), which includes the Si inside the eutectic structure. Hypereutectic Al-Si alloys are used for pistons and similar parts because the hard primary Si provides wear resistance, and treatments are applied to refine the primary Si.

phase-diagram-013.question: At constant pressure, a binary alloy is cooled from the liquid and its temperature-time relation (cooling curve) is recorded. In which case does the temperature stay constant during solidification (the curve becomes horizontal)?
choices: While an isomorphous alloy solidifies from the liquidus to the solidus
While an alloy of eutectic composition solidifies
While the primary phase crystallizes in a hypoeutectic alloy
phase-diagram-013.explanation: At constant pressure the phase rule for a binary system is F = C − P + 1. In an alloy of eutectic composition, solidification proceeds with three phases, the liquid and two solids, coexisting, so F = 2 − 3 + 1 = 0 and the temperature stays constant until solidification ends (as it does for a pure metal). In an isomorphous alloy, or during crystallization of the primary phase in a hypoeutectic alloy, two phases, liquid and solid, coexist, so F = 1 and solidification proceeds as the temperature falls and the phase compositions change. The cooling curve is then not horizontal; its slope becomes gentler because of the latent heat of solidification. In a hypoeutectic alloy this gentler section is followed by a horizontal section at the eutectic temperature, so the liquidus and eutectic temperatures can be read from the cooling curve.

phase-diagram-014.question: In a binary phase diagram, how is an intermetallic compound with a fixed composition ratio, such as Mg₂Si, represented?
choices: A compound with almost no solubility range is shown as a vertical line at its composition, with two-phase regions on either side
A compound is not a single phase but a fine mixture of the two component metals, so it does not appear on the phase diagram
A compound always melts at a lower temperature than both component metals, so it is shown as a single point, like a eutectic point
phase-diagram-014.explanation: An intermetallic compound is a single phase with a crystal structure different from those of its component metals. One with almost no composition range is drawn as a vertical line at its composition (for Mg₂Si, a 2:1 ratio of Mg to Si atoms), flanked by two-phase regions where the compound coexists with the neighboring phases. A compound such as Mg₂Si, which melts without changing composition (congruent melting) at a temperature above that of Mg, divides the diagram at its composition, so the diagram can be read as two eutectic diagrams, Mg-Mg₂Si and Mg₂Si-Si. Some intermediate phases have an appreciable composition range and appear as single-phase regions of finite width. The statements that the compound is a fine mixture and that it always melts at a lower temperature are wrong.

phase-diagram-015.question: A hypereutectoid steel with 1.2 wt%C is cooled under equilibrium to just below 727°C. Which is closest to the total mass fraction of cementite, proeutectoid cementite plus the cementite in the pearlite? Take the carbon content at 727°C as 0.022 wt%C for ferrite and 6.70 wt%C for cementite, and the eutectoid composition as 0.76 wt%C.
choices: About 7.4%
About 82%
About 18%
phase-diagram-015.explanation: Just below 727°C there are only two phases, ferrite and cementite, so the lever rule is applied between their compositions: W_Fe₃C = (1.2 − 0.022)/(6.70 − 0.022) = 1.178/6.678 ≈ 0.176, about 18%. About 7.4% is the fraction of proeutectoid cementite alone, found just above 727°C between austenite and cementite as (1.2 − 0.76)/(6.70 − 0.76) ≈ 0.074. Cementite is also present in the pearlite, so the total fraction is larger. About 82% corresponds to the ferrite fraction, 1 − 0.176. Whether a question asks for the fraction of a phase or of a microconstituent, such as a proeutectoid phase or pearlite, determines which compositions are used as the ends of the tie line.

phase-diagram-016.question: In a binary system at constant pressure there is an invariant reaction L₁ → α + L₂, in which, on cooling, a liquid L₁ of a certain composition splits into a solid α and another liquid L₂ of different composition. Which combination of the reaction's name and characteristic is correct?
choices: A peritectic reaction, in which a new solid forms as the liquid envelops the solid that crystallized first
A monotectic reaction, which appears in systems with a range where two liquids do not mix (a liquid miscibility gap)
A eutectic reaction, which produces a fine structure of two solids arranged in lamellae or rods
phase-diagram-016.explanation: L₁ → α + L₂ is a monotectic reaction. It appears at the bottom of a liquid miscibility gap, in systems whose two components do not mix at all compositions even as liquids and split into two liquids. The Cu-Pb system is a typical example; on solidification lead is dispersed in copper, a structure used in bearing alloys. Three phases coexist, so like the eutectic and peritectic it is an invariant reaction with zero degrees of freedom at constant pressure. The peritectic reaction is L + α → β, in which a liquid and a solid react to form another solid. The eutectic reaction is L → α + β, in which both products are solids.

phase-diagram-017.question: For an alloy in the α + L two-phase region of a binary system at constant pressure, which combination of the number of degrees of freedom and its meaning is correct?
choices: One degree of freedom: once the temperature is fixed, the compositions of α and of the liquid are each fixed
Two degrees of freedom: even at a fixed temperature, the composition of each phase changes with the overall alloy composition
Zero degrees of freedom: α and the liquid can coexist only at one particular temperature
phase-diagram-017.explanation: The phase rule for a binary system at constant pressure is F = C − P + 1, so in a two-phase region F = 2 − 2 + 1 = 1. Only one variable can be chosen freely, so fixing the temperature fixes the composition of α on the solidus and that of the liquid on the liquidus. This is why the ends of the tie line give the phase compositions; changing the overall composition at the same temperature changes only the amounts of the phases (the fractions from the lever rule). Zero degrees of freedom, restricted to one temperature, applies to invariant points such as the eutectic, where three phases coexist. Two degrees of freedom apply to single-phase regions.

phase-diagram-018.question: Which is closest to the eutectoid composition of the Fe-C system, 0.76 wt% C, converted to atomic percent? Take the atomic masses as 12.01 for C and 55.85 for Fe.
choices: About 0.16 at%
About 0.76 at%
About 3.4 at%
phase-diagram-018.explanation: For 100 g of alloy, C is 0.76/12.01 ≈ 0.0633 mol and Fe is 99.24/55.85 ≈ 1.777 mol, so the atomic fraction of C is 0.0633/(0.0633 + 1.777) ≈ 0.0344, about 3.4 at%. Carbon is much lighter than iron, so the same mass contains more atoms, and the atomic percent is more than four times the weight percent. About 0.16 at% multiplies by the atomic-mass ratio the wrong way round (0.76 × 12.01/55.85), and about 0.76 at% forgets to convert. Phase diagrams are drawn in either weight or atomic percent, so check which scale is used before reading one.

phase-diagram-019.question: The Fe-C system has two phase diagrams, the Fe-Fe₃C diagram and the Fe-graphite diagram. Which statement about their relationship is correct?
choices: Fe₃C is the stable phase, and graphite is a metastable phase that appears only when Si is added
Fe₃C is metastable and the true stable equilibrium is Fe-graphite, but graphite forms only with difficulty in steels
They are the same diagram, differing only in whether carbon is expressed in weight percent or atomic percent
phase-diagram-019.explanation: Graphite is the thermodynamically stable phase and Fe₃C is metastable. Nucleating and growing graphite, however, requires long-range diffusion of carbon, so Fe₃C forms first when ordinary steels cool, and in practice the Fe-Fe₃C diagram is used. Si promotes graphite formation, so in cast irons with high Si, graphite crystallizes according to the Fe-graphite diagram. Holding a high-carbon steel at high temperature for a long time can decompose the cementite into graphite (graphitization), a sign that Fe₃C is metastable. The two diagrams also differ slightly in their eutectic and eutectoid temperatures and compositions; the difference is not one of units.

phase-diagram-020.question: In the Al-Cu system the solubility of Cu in Al reaches its maximum of about 5.65 wt% at 548°C and falls with decreasing temperature to a very small value near room temperature. Which condition on the Cu content is correct for an alloy to be precipitation-hardened by solution treatment, quenching and aging?
choices: The closer it is to the eutectic composition (about 33 wt% Cu), the more precipitate forms on aging and the greater the hardening
The more it exceeds the maximum solubility, the more Cu dissolves in solution treatment and the greater the hardening
It lies below the maximum solubility and above the solubility at the aging temperature
phase-diagram-020.explanation: Precipitation hardening needs a composition that becomes a single-phase solid solution at high temperature (solution treatment) and is supersaturated beyond the solubility limit at low temperature. In Al-Cu, a Cu content below the maximum solubility of about 5.65 wt% can be fully dissolved by solution treatment, and a content above the solubility at the aging temperature lets the supersaturated Cu precipitate finely. This is why practical 2000-series alloys contain a few percent Cu. Cu beyond the maximum solubility does not dissolve during solution treatment and remains as coarse Al₂Cu that lowers toughness. An alloy near the eutectic composition is mostly eutectic structure and cannot be made a solid solution by solution treatment.

phase-diagram-021.question: In the Pb–Sn system (eutectic temperature 183 °C, solubility limit of Sn in α at that temperature 18.3 wt%), an alloy with 10 wt% Sn is cooled slowly from the liquid. Assume the solubility limit of α decreases as temperature falls, ending well below 10 wt% Sn at room temperature. Which describes the room-temperature microstructure?
choices: A mixture of primary α and eutectic structure formed from liquid remaining at the eutectic temperature
First all α; once the solubility limit is exceeded, β precipitates within the α grains and on their boundaries
All α solid solution that stays unchanged down to room temperature, giving a single-phase α structure
phase-diagram-021.explanation: Since 10 wt% Sn is below the 18.3 wt% solubility limit of α at the eutectic temperature, the alloy passes between the liquidus and solidus and finishes solidifying as all α solid solution. No liquid survives to the eutectic temperature, so no eutectic forms. On further cooling, the solubility limit of α falls with temperature, so once the alloy crosses the solvus line it becomes supersaturated in Sn and β precipitates within the α grains and on their boundaries. The room-temperature structure is therefore β dispersed in α, not a single phase. Primary α plus eutectic forms in hypoeutectic alloys of 18.3–61.9 wt% Sn. A solubility limit that falls with temperature is the same principle used in precipitation hardening.

phase-diagram-022.question: Eutectic or near-eutectic compositions are often chosen for solders and casting alloys. What is the reason?
choices: They melt at the system's lowest temperature and freeze at a single temperature, so there is no mushy range and fluidity is good
At the eutectic composition primary crystals grow large during solidification, and the coarse grains give the highest strength and ductility
A eutectic alloy melts at the same temperature as the higher-melting component metal, so the joints it makes can be used at high temperature
phase-diagram-022.explanation: An alloy of eutectic composition solidifies at the eutectic point where the liquidus and solidus meet, so it freezes at the lowest temperature in the system and, like a pure metal, at a single temperature. With no range in which solid and liquid coexist as a slush, the molten alloy flows well and fills gaps and every corner of a mold, and hot cracking and segregation during solidification are less likely. In the Sn–Pb system the eutectic composition of 61.9 wt% Sn melts at 183 °C and has long been used for solder. At the eutectic composition no primary crystals form; the result is a fine eutectic structure of two solid phases, so the statement about coarse primary crystals is wrong. The eutectic melts below both component metals, so the statement that it matches the higher melting point is also wrong.

phase-diagram-023.question: A slowly cooled hypoeutectoid steel examined under the microscope shows 25% pearlite by area. Taking the area fraction as equal to the mass fraction, with the eutectoid composition at 727 °C as 0.76 wt% C, the carbon content of ferrite as 0.022 wt% C and cementite as 6.70 wt% C, which is closest to the carbon content of this steel?
choices: About 1.7 wt% C
About 0.58 wt% C
About 0.21 wt% C
phase-diagram-023.explanation: Just above 727 °C, proeutectoid ferrite (0.022 wt% C) coexists with austenite (0.76 wt% C) that will become pearlite. The pearlite fraction is W_P = (C₀ − 0.022)/(0.76 − 0.022), so C₀ = 0.022 + 0.25 × 0.738 ≈ 0.21 wt% C. About 0.58 wt% C swaps the pearlite and ferrite fractions and uses 0.75. About 1.7 wt% C applies the tie line between ferrite and cementite, confusing pearlite, a microconstituent, with cementite, a phase. Because ferrite and pearlite have nearly the same density, estimating carbon content from area fractions in this way is a common rule of thumb in examining steel microstructures.

phase-diagram-024.question: Transformation temperatures of steel are written with symbols such as Ac₃ and Ar₃. Which correctly relates them to the equilibrium transformation temperature A₃ shown on the phase diagram?
choices: Ac₃ on heating lies above the equilibrium A₃ and Ar₃ on cooling lies below it, and the gaps grow with faster heating or cooling
Ac₃ on heating lies below the equilibrium A₃ and Ar₃ on cooling lies above it, so transformation occurs before equilibrium is reached
Ac₃ and Ar₃ always equal the equilibrium A₃; c denotes values for high-carbon steels and r values for low-carbon steels
phase-diagram-024.explanation: The c and r come from the French words for heating (chauffage) and cooling (refroidissement). A transformation needs a departure from the equilibrium temperature to create a driving force, and nucleation and carbon diffusion take time, so the transformation is observed above the equilibrium A₃ on heating and below it on cooling. Hence Ac₃ > A₃ > Ar₃, and likewise for A₁. The faster the heating or cooling, the more the transformation lags and the larger the gap. Saying the transformation starts before the equilibrium temperature reverses the directions of superheating and undercooling. Because phase-diagram lines are equilibrium values, the shift caused by heating rate is also considered when setting heat-treatment temperatures.

phase-diagram-025.question: Consider an isothermal section, at one temperature, of a ternary phase diagram at constant pressure. Which statement about an alloy lying inside a triangular region where three phases coexist (a tie triangle) is correct?
choices: One degree of freedom remains after fixing temperature, so the compositions of the three phases shift continuously as the alloy composition changes
Fixing temperature leaves zero freedom: the three phase compositions are the triangle's corners, and alloy composition changes only the phase fractions
Three phases coexist only at invariant points, so no triangular region appears in an isothermal section and the three phases meet at a single point
phase-diagram-025.explanation: At constant pressure the phase rule is F = C − P + 1, so for three coexisting phases in a ternary system (C = 3), F = 3 − 3 + 1 = 1. Fixing the temperature uses up this freedom, so the compositions of the three phases are fixed at that temperature and appear as the three corners of a triangle in the isothermal section. Every alloy inside the triangle splits into the same three phases; only the amounts change with alloy composition, found from the center-of-gravity relation within the triangle (an extension of the lever rule). Because three-phase coexistence in a ternary spans a range of temperature, triangular regions appear in isothermal sections. Do not confuse this with a binary system, where three-phase coexistence is an invariant point.
